newsitem.title: USA: Dollar mixed after comments from German and U.S. officials.
newsitem.headline: Dollar mixed after comments from German and U.S. officials.

text.p: NEW YORK, April 17 - The dollar fell versus the mark on Thursday after Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said the German central bank does not want the German currency to weaken further.

But the dollar edged higher against the Japanese yen despite reports showing deterioration in the United States' trade position relative to Japan. Remarks by a Commerce Department official helped soothe concern that the strong dollar was to blame for the trade figures.
The dollar also gained as investors continued to buy the currency to take advantage of the fact that interest rates in the United States remain well above those in Japan.

During a news conference after the Bundesbank council's regularly scheduled meeting on Thursday, Tietmeyer said the mark's current level on foreign exchange markets correctly reflects economic fundamentals.
He also said the central bank does not want a weak mark, but remains interested in having a strong mark.
The dollar slid toward 1.7200 marks after the Tietmeyer statements reached currency markets.

The Tietmeyer comments were "a moderate statement of support for the mark," said Kevin Harris, an international economist at MCM CurrencyWatch. "If they don't want it weaker, the two things that can happen are that it stays where it is or it gets stronger. And currencies rarely stay where they are."
In late New York trading, the dollar settled at 1.7238 marks, down from 1.7285 marks on Wednesday. The dollar rose to 125.98 yen from 125.75 yen.
Against other currencies, the dollar fell to 1.4637 Swiss francs from 1.4720 francs, but climbed to Canadian $1.4005 from C$1.3972. The British pound rose to $1.6295 from $1.6247.

Initially, the dollar came under selling pressure overnight in Asia after the Japanese Ministry of Finance reported that Japan's trade surplus with the United States ballooned 11.2 percent in March from a year earlier. By comparison, the overall Japanese customs-cleared trade surplus shrank 26.8 percent in March from a year ago.

Japanese trade figures were followed on Thursday morning by a report from the Commerce Department showing the U.S. trade deficit with Japan widened slightly in February from January. But the overall U.S. trade gap narrowed 8.5 percent to $11.59 billion in February, wider than the $10.1 billion shortfall expected by Wall Street economists.
Still, Commerce undersecretary Everett Ehrlich told Reuters Financial Television that the dollar was not a major factor driving the trade figures.
The dollar, which had managed to inch up after the U.S. trade report, rose slightly higher after Ehrlich's remarks.

"To an extent, maybe there was a little bit of movement on Ehrlich," said David Solin, a partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics. He noted an ongoing interest to buy dollars and sell yen, adding: "Again obviously, that's due to the big, wide (interest) rate differentials."

The Bank of Japan has kept its official interest rates at record low levels to stimulate economic growth, but the Federal Reserve hiked the federal funds rate to 5.50 percent from 5.25 percent in March to keep inflationary pressures in check. Higher interest rates typically help the dollar by making deposits denominated in the currency more attractive to foreign investors.
